title: Duke Ellington wrote for his players and loved his band
summary: Ellington wrote for players once he knew their strengths, called the band his toy, and kept touring after paying his dues.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: And Duke didn't want Willie to leave. But Duke told us once that he's just learning what Willie was doing to write right for him just before he left, you know. Because he had a good spot with Duke. You know, Duke would write for you. That's one thing. If you stayed with Duke long enough for him to see what your style was, he would write for you. Because he wrote for all the guys in that band.
Especially the ones who stayed around him for a while. He sure wrote for Rex. I told Rex, I said nobody

will ever write for you like that again. He said I know it, you know. They knew it. They knew it. But Duke would have to hear you long enough to know exactly what you were doing, what your strong points were and your weak points. You'd have to be with him that long. He wouldn't do it right away. You'd have to be with him for a while before he did it.
I think he got inspiration from the players he wrote for. I mean inspiration for the things he wrote other than the showcases for the soloists.
He would get excited about something a singer sang, or some particular solo, the way it was played.
Oh well, that was his toy. He told everybody that was his plaything, that was his hobby, that was his toy. And it was.
Because he didn't have to go through all of that in years later, all those one-nighters and all that drudgery out there. He didn't have to do it but he loved it, he enjoyed it.
Yeah, he -- I admired him an awful lot for that too because knowing that he had paid enough dues not
to ever go through all of that again, and he still continued to do it.
